# AI Coding Assistants

The RZMPS skill helps coding assistants create and debug Three.js particle systems and VFX,
compose emitters, modules, spatial effects, and renderers, and validate WebGL and WebGPU
output using actual canvas previews. The complete skill lives in the public GitHub repository
at [.agents/skills/rzmps](https://github.com/rzmay/rzmps/tree/HEAD/.agents/skills/rzmps).
Its entry point and references are generated from these canonical human guides and API declarations.

## Installation

Choose an installation explicitly after reviewing the skill and authorizing any changes to
agent configuration. Installing `@rzmps/rzmps` with npm never installs a skill automatically.

<!-- distribution:installation:start -->
```bash
# Discover available skills
npx skills add rzmay/rzmps --list

# Install the RZMPS skill
npx skills add rzmay/rzmps --skill rzmps

# Install globally (optional)
npx skills add rzmay/rzmps --skill rzmps -g
```
<!-- distribution:installation:end -->

The CLI lets you select compatible agents. Project installation affects the current project;
`-g` installs at user scope. The skill follows the [Agent Skills format](https://agentskills.io/specification).
Compatible installers discover it directly from GitHub; no manual registry submission is required.
See the [skills CLI documentation](https://github.com/vercel-labs/skills) for agent selection and installation options.

These shorthand commands read the repository's default branch. They become available once
this skill is committed and published there. Before that, test the actual checkout with
`npx skills add . --list`, or use a published branch URL such as
`https://github.com/rzmay/rzmps/tree/develop` in place of `rzmay/rzmps`.
Local validation does not prove that unpushed files are already discoverable from GitHub.

## Lightweight npm Guidance

<!-- distribution:npm-readme:start -->
The optional [RZMPS skill](https://github.com/rzmay/rzmps/tree/HEAD/.agents/skills/rzmps)
helps coding assistants build Three.js particle systems and VFX using emitters, modules,
renderers, and WebGL/WebGPU previews.

```bash
npx skills add rzmay/rzmps --skill rzmps
```

Review the skill and authorize installation before changing agent configuration.
The npm package includes a short generated `AGENTS.md`, without bundling the full skill or
its references. These entry points do not guarantee automatic agent discovery. For the
installed version's API, inspect `build/index.d.ts` and the package version; see the
[canonical documentation](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/) for guides.
<!-- distribution:npm-readme:end -->

## Discovery and Maintenance

The repository, this documentation site, the npm README, and generated `llms.txt` all point
to the same canonical skill in GitHub. `llms.txt` includes explicit installation guidance;
the website does not host another copy of the skill or its bundled references.

`llms-full.txt` is an optional generated Markdown bundle of the guides, examples, and API
reference for tools that need a complete documentation snapshot. It is a convenience format,
not a requirement for skill discovery, installation, or automatic agent access. Prefer the
index and relevant pages when the full bundle is unnecessary.

`npm run docs:generate` refreshes agent references, documentation discovery files, npm `AGENTS.md`,
and README guidance blocks. `npm run agents:check` validates frontmatter and reference links,
discovers and installs the checkout skill in a temporary project, and audits `npm pack --dry-run`.
It leaves consumer projects and the user's agent configuration untouched.

The entire `.agents/skills/rzmps` folder remains committed so GitHub installers can fetch it
without running a build. Its `SKILL.md` is generated from the definition below, and its reference
pages come from the guides, examples, and API declarations. Website indexes and `llms` files
are ignored build artifacts, regenerated for local builds and deployment. CI checks that the
committed skill matches its canonical sources; it does not automatically commit changes.

Run `npm run agents:check -- --github` to test the exact public shorthand discovery command.
CI checks GitHub commit URLs after pushes and the shorthand after publishing to the default
branch; pull requests validate their checkout without assuming the proposed skill is already public.

## Canonical Skill Definition

The following metadata and workflow generate `.agents/skills/rzmps/SKILL.md`. Edit them here;
the generated skill rewrites documentation links to bundled references so it remains portable.

<!-- skill:metadata:start -->
```yaml
name: rzmps
description: Build and debug Three.js particle systems and VFX in RZMPS using emitters, modules, renderers, and WebGL/WebGPU canvas previews.
```
<!-- skill:metadata:end -->

<!-- skill:instructions:start -->
Inspect the installed package version and public exports before using a feature. In this repository, use the current branch's TypeScript source. Prefer existing emitters, modules, renderers, and spatial effects before adding custom behavior.

Read [getting started](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-particle-system.html) for scene ownership and updates, [concepts](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/concepts.html) for lifecycle, priority, tags, spatial collections, and subsystem composition, and [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) before implementing TSL callbacks, readback, collision, or spatial-grid behavior. Search the [generated API](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/api/index.html) for signatures.

Reuse a canonical factory from `examples/`; inspect [example explanations](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/index.html) for its configuration rationale. Preserve the default factory and author metadata contracts. Add balanced documentation source regions and update the authored Markdown explanation, then run `npm run docs:generate` and `npm run docs:check`.

Check the selected renderer and custom material compatibility using [compatibility](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/compatibility.html). Build packages, run `npm run preview -- --example <id> --backend webgl`, and inspect the contact sheet and metadata. Repeat with webgpu when relevant; report unavailable backends explicitly. Adjust warmup, interval, or scene to capture the actual event. Technical success alone does not establish visual quality.

Update root systems once; parents own subsystem timing. Follow Module, Renderer, Emitter, and SpatialEffect CPU/GPU extension hooks and priority semantics. Do not treat WebGPU rendering as proof of GPU simulation; check component support and `isGPUProcessingActive`. Use features present in the installed version and current branch. Reference files are generated from human documentation; edit their canonical source instead.

Repository preview scripts and `examples/` are checkout tools. In a consumer project, adapt an example to its existing rendering loop or use a repository checkout for previews; do not assume consumers have repository npm scripts. Read the [installation guidance](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/ai-coding-assistants.html#installation) before installing the skill or changing agent configuration.
<!-- skill:instructions:end -->

These measurements describe one machine and browser, rather than a performance guarantee. Particle count, modules, geometry, resolution, and hardware all affect results. Simulation-only cases still run in a browser render loop; their particle renderer does no drawing.

## Running Benchmarks

From the repository root, install dependencies with `npm ci`, then run:

```sh
npm run benchmark:run
# Refresh the root and npm README tables from a new local measurement:
npm run benchmark:update-report
# Regenerate this page and the agent references from the README report:
npm run docs:generate
# Export a measurement without changing the published table:
npm run benchmark:export -- /tmp/rzmps-benchmark.json
```

The default run uses a headless, uncapped browser at 1280×720. Set `RZMPS_BENCHMARK_DURATION_MS` and `RZMPS_BENCHMARK_WARMUP_MS` to change measurement windows. Use `npm run benchmark:run -- --vsync` for browser frame pacing or `--headed` to view the run.

Average update time measures `ParticleSystem.update()`; frame time includes the render loop. The 1% low FPS is the reciprocal of the average of the slowest 1% of measured frames. P99 frame time is reported separately. The Particles column shows the measured population, with a minimum–maximum range for workloads such as spawn churn that change population during measurement.

## Pull Request Comparisons

CI builds and runs the complete benchmark page from each revision against its matching library. Three samples per revision run in interleaved ABBAAB order; the comparison uses the median for each metric and includes only case names present in both revisions.

GitHub-hosted runners use software WebGL. The CI profile uses a 640×360 viewport, browser frame pacing, and a 2,000-particle low polygon box workload for the mesh case. Its results are useful for relative comparisons on that runner and should be interpreted separately from the published hardware results above. Completed samples, environment metadata, and available timeout diagnostics are uploaded as workflow artifacts even when a run fails.

# Collision and Physics

The base package includes `ThreeCollisionBackend`, which raycasts against a
Three.js scene.

For GPU processing, `Collision` automatically selects `ThreeGPUCollisionBackend` when no backend
is supplied. It uses packed `three-mesh-bvh` acceleration data and distinguishes static,
transform-dynamic, and geometry-dynamic scene meshes. Supplying an explicit CPU physics backend
makes the collision module GPU-incompatible, and applying impulses to scene bodies remains a CPU
feature. See [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) before choosing an explicit backend.

See the generated API for constructor options and defaults.

The `ThreeCollisionBackend` uses two octrees for static and dynamic collisions.
Sorting objects into static and dynamic can be done automatically, or with
supporting identifiers passed into the constructor options. Explicitly stated
`staticObjects` and `dynamicObjects` lists are treated as the source of truth if
present.

If explicit lists are not provided, the scene is traversed and the
`staticObjectFilter`, `dynamicObjectFilter`, and `objectFilter` predicates are
used to select objects. `objectFilter` selects whether objects are included at
all but does not decide what is considered static or dynamic.

If none of these predicates are provided, the octrees are automatically
constructed from the scene traversal, with distinctions between static and
dynamic objects being made based on movement in the scene.

For external physics engines, use the extension packages:

| Package         | Engine       | npm                                                                            |
| --------------- | ------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `@rzmps/rapier` | Rapier       | [npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/rapier](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/rapier) |
| `@rzmps/jolt`   | Jolt Physics | [npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/jolt](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/jolt)     |
| `@rzmps/ammo`   | Ammo.js      | [npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/ammo](https://www.npmjs.com/package/@rzmps/ammo)     |

```ts
import { Collision } from "@rzmps/rzmps";
import { RapierCollisionBackend } from "@rzmps/rapier";

const collision = new Collision({
  backend: new RapierCollisionBackend({ RAPIER, world }),
  bounce: 0.6,
  dampen: 0.1,
  radiusScale: 1,
  lifetimeLoss: 0.2,
  applyImpulses: true,
});
```

Physics backends receive an existing physics world. They do not create, step, or
own the physics simulation.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/concepts.md -->

# Composition and Lifecycle

A `ParticleSystem` owns arrays of emitters, modules, renderers, and explicitly selected spatial effects. These are mutable collections; use `addEmitter`, `addModule`, `addRenderer`, and their removal methods when changing composition so setup and cleanup hooks run. Passing a single component to the constructor is also supported. Constructor options may be copied to instance fields, so changing an options object later does not always reconfigure a component. Check the exposed runtime property and its source before relying on live edits.

An emitter chooses where particles are born, their initial values, tags, and birth times. `rate` is particles per second; `rateOverDistance` adds emission based on source movement. A burst fires when its time is crossed. Lifetimes are seconds, while lifetime module callbacks receive normalized age from zero to one. A two-element array usually defines a sampled range; a `Set` selects a discrete value. Consult the exported dynamic-value types when supplying callbacks.

Each update restores cached permanent values, prepares modules once, sorts modifiers into priority phases, integrates particles, then sends the resulting particle list to renderers. [Module priority](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/module-priority.html) explains which changes persist. Renderers can share one simulated population: a sprite, trail, light, and sound can all represent the same particle. [Tags](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/tags.html) select subsets without duplicating simulation.

`start()` starts playback and resets the emission cycle, including when restarting a paused system. `pause()` freezes simulation. `stop(clearParticles)` stops emission and resets system time; surviving particles can continue moving on subsequent updates when they are retained. `destroy()` permanently releases owned resources. Removing a system from its scene performs temporary cleanup so it can be attached elsewhere. Call `destroy()` when you will no longer use it.

The loop duration schedules emission; it is independent of each particle's lifetime. Turning looping off does not necessarily delete existing particles: `endBehavior` determines what happens after the duration. A population estimate for constant emission is rate multiplied by average lifetime, before bursts, culling, or subsystems. These are nominal estimates: timestep quantization and emission scheduling can lower the observed count. Set `maxParticles` to bound simulation costs, and remember that each renderer adds work.

[Subsystems](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/subsystems.html) attach secondary effects to lifecycle events. [Spatial effects and collections](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/spatial-effects.html) coordinate scene-wide behavior. Both rendering backends use this same composition model; see [compatibility](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/compatibility.html) and [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html).

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/decals.md -->

# Surface Decals

`DecalRenderer` clips persistent geometry onto rigid scene meshes with Three.js `DecalGeometry`. Pass a material first
and an optional options object. Each mark owns a material clone and geometry; your material, textures, and target
geometry remain caller-owned. Standard Three.js materials work with WebGL and WebGPU rendering.

```ts
import * as THREE from 'three';
import { DecalRenderer } from '@rzmps/rzmps';

const material = new THREE.MeshBasicMaterial({ color: '#542710' });
const decals = new DecalRenderer(material, {
  direction: new THREE.Vector3(0, -1, 0),
  maxDistance: 2,
  depth: 0.1,
  size: 1,
  lifetime: 8,
  opacity: t => 1 - t,
});
// Supply decals in a ParticleSystem's renderers collection.
```

Spawn projection is enabled by default. Set `onSpawn: false, onCollision: true` for contact marks, or `onDeath: true` to
search from the final particle position. Triggers are independent; enabling two can deliberately create two sets of
marks for one particle. `continuousRate` defaults to zero (disabled). Set `onSpawn: false, continuousRate: 2` to project
from each live particle twice per second instead of waiting for a collision. Its first projection occurs after one
interval, so a particle that dies sooner than `1 / continuousRate` never projects continuously. Birth, collision, and
death switches still work independently when continuous placement is enabled.

Continuous placement follows particle simulation age, respects tag filters, and stops when the particle dies. Pause
freezes placement and decal aging; stopping emission without clearing lets surviving particles keep projecting. Repeated
processing of the same particle snapshot does not duplicate an interval. If a large step crosses multiple intervals,
missed projections use the current particle state, with catch-up work limited to `maxDecals` per particle per update.
Clear/reset discard timing history; attaching to an already living population does not replay its entire past. Emitters,
bursts, distance-based emission, and subsystems continue to determine which particles exist.

`ratio` defaults to `1` and is clamped to `[0, 1]`. It selects a consistent fraction of particles by ID for all
projection triggers, including continuous placement. Setting it to zero disables new projections; existing decals
continue fading.

Constructor settings are exposed directly as renderer properties, for example `decals.continuousRate = 2` or
`decals.size = 1.5`; there is no stored options object. New configuration affects subsequent projections, while existing
marks keep their creation-time properties. Numeric configuration is clamped instead of throwing: distance and depth
remain positive, capacities/counts are rounded down, capacity/rate cannot be negative, and nonfinite values use defaults
(or zero for an explicit invalid hit count). Radial ray counts are rounded down to at least one, with nonfinite counts
becoming one.

Directions are world-space vectors. The exported `DecalDirectionSampler` and `DecalHitSelection` types describe
direction and selection callbacks. A direction callback receives the original particle in its simulation space and may
return one vector or an ordered array. Nonzero finite vectors are normalized without modifying them.
`DecalRenderer.Radial(24)` returns twenty-four deterministic Fibonacci-sphere directions. Local particle positions are
transformed into world space before querying.

`DecalRenderer.Forward()` samples local +Y transformed by `particle.rotation`, matching the forward-axis convention in
`OrientToDirection`. Its optional `THREE.Vector3` supplies an XYZ rotation offset in radians, applied in the particle's
local frame before its rotation. For example, rotate X by π to point backward:

```ts
const decals = new DecalRenderer(material, {
  direction: DecalRenderer.Forward(new THREE.Vector3(Math.PI, 0, 0)),
});
```

Forward follows orientation; use `OrientToDirection` when orientation should follow velocity. As with any particle-aware
sampler, a rotated local simulation needs a callback that transforms the returned direction to world space using the
system's world matrix. Samplers leave particle state and caller-owned vectors unchanged.

Each ray contributes its first supported intersection. Search uses a configured `ThreeCollisionBackend`'s current
membership, including explicit object lists and filters; without that backend it scans scene meshes using the shared
collision exclusions. Particle renderer objects and decal meshes are excluded. Other physics backends supply contacts
directly when their `CollisionHit.object` is a supported mesh; otherwise search falls back to scene geometry. A valid
collision contact bypasses direction sampling and raycasting. When mesh identity is unavailable, a finite nonzero
collision normal selects the opposite world-space search direction, including on walls and slopes; the configured
sampler is used only when that normal is unavailable. The built-in octree backend currently lacks target identity, so it
uses this fallback, which can differ from an aggregate capsule contact.

`maxDistance` limits ray length in world units (default 2). `depth` is the projector's Z clipping thickness (default
0.1); width and height come from `size` and inherited X/Y scale. Normals use the mesh normal matrix, and particle Z
rotation supplies projector roll in radians. `offset` displaces generated vertices along the outgoing normal (default
0.001). Keep depth shallow on thin or curved targets: clipping can reach nearby faces and corners can distort the
projection.

`hitSelection` defaults to the direct callback `DecalRenderer.Nearest`. It receives `(hits, particle, maxHits)`, with
`THREE.Intersection` candidates in ray order. `face.normal` and optional `normal` follow Three.js mesh-local
conventions; transform them with the target's normal matrix for world-space comparisons.

| Selector | Omitted maxHits | Explicit maxHits: 4 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `DecalRenderer.Nearest` | One closest | Up to four closest |
| `DecalRenderer.Farthest` | One farthest | Up to four farthest |
| `DecalRenderer.All` | All in ray order | First four in ray order |

The built-ins leave the input array unchanged. Negative `maxHits` disables truncation; zero creates no marks. A custom
selector may return fewer candidates. Explicit nonnegative `maxHits` also caps its valid result. Distinct intersections
on one mesh remain separate candidates.

```ts
const decals = new DecalRenderer(material, {
  direction: DecalRenderer.Radial(24),
  maxHits: 4,
  hitSelection: (hits, particle, maxHits) => {
    const upward = hits.filter(hit => {
      const normal = (hit.normal ?? hit.face?.normal)?.clone();
      if (!normal) return false;
      normal.applyMatrix3(new THREE.Matrix3().getNormalMatrix(hit.object.matrixWorld)).normalize();
      return normal.y > 0.5;
    });
    return DecalRenderer.Nearest(upward, particle, maxHits);
  },
});
```

`color` accepts `ColorInput` values (Three.js colors, CSS strings, or numeric hex values). `size` accepts
`Vector3Input`: a number for uniform width/height or a vector for separate X/Y dimensions; Z is ignored because `depth`
controls clipping. Both support callbacks, ranges, and sets without modifying caller-owned values.

`size`, `color`, and `lifetime` use the existing CPU `DynamicValue` helpers and are sampled once at source particle age.
Geometry never resizes after creation. Nonpositive or nonfinite lifetime/size creates nothing. Lifetime is in seconds;
its default is eight. `opacity` is evaluated on normalized **decal age** from zero to one, with a stable source seed for
random ranges. It multiplies the template material opacity and snapshotted alpha. CPU evaluation does not accept TSL
nodes.

`inheritColor`, `inheritScale`, and `inheritAlpha` default to 1 and follow subsystem math: base multiplied by `lerp(1,
particleValue, amount)`, component-wise for color and nonuniform scale. Zero and negative amounts retain the base value,
matching subsystem handling. Half blends halfway, and one inherits fully. The material color, configured color, and
inherited particle color multiply together. Each decal's material fades independently.

`distanceAffectsSize` and `distanceAffectsOpacity` default to zero. Their multiplier is `lerp(1, proximity, amount)`,
where `proximity = 1 - clamp(hit.distance / maxDistance, 0, 1)`. Zero is neutral and one gives full distance
attenuation.

`maxHits` limits selection per trigger. `maxDecals` instead limits active persistent marks (default 256). Insertion at
capacity evicts the oldest mark and disposes its geometry and cloned material. Expiry, `clear`, reset, removal from the
scene, and destruction also release owned resources. Pause freezes decal age; stopping without clearing lets marks
continue fading. Destruction unregisters callbacks. Renderer update/count LOD does not skip lifetime updates or
lifecycle placement; tag filters still apply. Normal system simulation LOD and culling affect the system clock as usual.

Generated geometry is stored in the target mesh's local space so it follows rigid motion. Skinned and instanced targets
are rejected; deforming geometry and animated morph targets are unsupported. Choose a material with a color property
when using tint inheritance. Texture and custom shader compatibility follow the supplied material's capabilities.

GPU event-only modes use the existing asynchronous lifecycle-event snapshots without adding particle readbacks.
Continuous mode uses the same `updateCPUFromGPU` helper as LightRenderer and TrailRenderer, forwarding snapshots through
the normal update path. There is no separate readback-frequency cap; the helper guards against overlapping requests.
Fixed direction vectors request position, rotation, normalized age, and elapsed age, plus scale/color/alpha when
inherited. Arbitrary direction callbacks may inspect every particle field, so those request complete snapshots. Decal
lifetimes still advance on each simulation update while a readback is in flight. Marks may appear after readback
latency. GPU contacts currently lack mesh identity and search opposite the collision normal. Follow-up work: preserve
GPU collision target identity for exact contact projection. Geometry clipping and material allocation remain CPU work;
batching and deforming mesh projection are deferred.

The [Splatter example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/splatter.html) uses matte paintballs and long-lived collision marks that inherit color
and scale. The [Fire example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fire.html) uses continuous radial projection from its flame particles.
Short-lived, low-opacity marks fade in and accumulate into textured scorch patches. [Fireball](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireball.html)
uses the same texture with a higher continuous rate suited to its brief bursts.

## Emitting from Persistent Decals

Set `emissionTags: ['acid-pool']` to register each successful decal as an emission source.
The public `decals` collection exposes `decal.source`; call `decal.source?.emitEvent('bubble', payload)`
from application scheduling code. Sources follow decal transforms, rigid surface movement, material
color and opacity, and are disposed on expiry, eviction, clear or renderer destruction.
A child with `{ tags: ['acid-pool'], emitContinuous: true, inheritLifetime: 0 }` can emit smoke
from every pool; another with `onEvent: ['bubble']` can produce splashes.

See [Emission Sources and Custom Events](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/emission-sources-events.html) for handle APIs and deferred
synchronization, and [Acid](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/acid.html) for the complete effect.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/development.md -->

# Local Development

Clone the repository and install dependencies:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/rzmay/rzmps.git
cd rzmps
npm install
```

Run the demo and documentation together, with package watchers:

```bash
npm run dev
```

The command generates the documentation sources and builds the packages, then serves
the demo at `http://localhost:5173/`. Preview images are generated while the demo is
available. Documentation starts at `http://localhost:5173/docs/` once previews finish.
During preview generation, documentation requests return a temporary 503 response.

Use `npm run docs:dev` for the same startup sequence without package watchers.
`npm run docs:generate` still generates both documentation sources and previews;
`npm run docs:generate -- --skip-previews` defers previews to `npm run docs:previews`.

Preview images and their manifest in `apps/docs/public/previews/` are ignored build
artifacts. Documentation builds regenerate missing or stale previews using Puppeteer;
CI installs Chrome before building. Local captures are reused while their inputs match.

Build the core package:

```bash
npm run build --workspace packages/rzmps
```

Run the package in watch mode:

```bash
npm run dev --workspace packages/rzmps
```

Run the demo locally:

```bash
npm start --workspace apps/demo
```

Build the demo:

```bash
npm run build --workspace apps/demo
```

Build the physics extensions:

```bash
npm run build --workspace @rzmps/rapier
npm run build --workspace @rzmps/jolt
npm run build --workspace @rzmps/ammo
```

Build all publishable packages:

```bash
npm run build:modules
```

Run the core library regression tests:

```bash
npm test
```

The test suite lives in `packages/rzmps/tests` and focuses on behavior that is
easy to regress while optimizing internals: force application, priority phases,
depth and size mapping, distortion controls, audio effect calculations,
mutable-value isolation, and subsystem inheritance.

Run the benchmark suite and print browser-rendered results to the terminal:

```bash
npm run benchmark:run
```

Benchmark runs disable browser frame-rate limiting by default. Add `-- --vsync`
to measure refresh-rate-bound behavior instead.

Open a visible browser window while running the same benchmark:

```bash
npm run benchmark:run -- --open
```

Serve the built benchmark page for visual/manual inspection:

```bash
npm run benchmark:serve --workspace demo
```

Then open `http://127.0.0.1:4173/?benchmark=1`.

Update the benchmark report tables in the READMEs:

```bash
npm run benchmark:update-report
```

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/dynamic-values.md -->

# Dynamic Values

Many RZMPS options use `DynamicValue<T>`.

```ts
type DynamicValue<T> =
  | T
  | ((t: number) => DynamicValue<T>)
  | [DynamicValue<T>, DynamicValue<T>]
  | Set<DynamicValue<T>>;

// Used for parameters that can take multiple elements or just one
type Multiple<T> = T | T[];

// Multiple with least one value
type StrictMultiple<T> = T | [T, ...[T]];

// In RZMPS, tags are natively strings
type Tag = string;
```

Lifetime-module callbacks receive normalized particle age, from `0` to `1`. Emitter rate and birth-value callbacks
instead receive normalized emission-cycle time. A callback is evaluated in its component’s context; it does not receive
wall-clock seconds.

| Form           | Example                       | Behavior                               |
| -------------- | ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| Static value   | `2`                           | Always returns the same value.         |
| Function       | `(t) => 1 - t`                | Re-evaluates over normalized lifetime. |
| Two-item array | `[0.5, 2]`                    | Random value between min and max.      |
| Set            | `new Set(["spark", "smoke"])` | Random choice.                         |

Dynamic values are supported for numbers, vectors, and colors where the option
type uses `DynamicValue<number>`, `DynamicValue<THREE.Vector3>`, or
`DynamicValue<THREE.Color>`.

Color inputs accept `THREE.Color`, hex numbers, and CSS color strings (the same values
as `new THREE.Color(...)`). Uniform-axis inputs such as scale, scale velocity/acceleration,
noise strength, rotation/angular velocity/angular acceleration, and velocity limits also accept a number: `scale: 2`
means
`new THREE.Vector3(2, 2, 2)`. Positions and directional inputs still require vectors.
These shortcuts work inside callbacks, ranges, and sets too, including GPU processing;
particle state always contains `THREE.Color` and `THREE.Vector3` objects.

```ts
initialValues: {
  color: new Set(["#ff8844", 0xffcc00]),
  scale: [0.1, 0.5],
}
// Lifetime modifier: scale: (t) => 1 + t
```

## Rotation Shortcuts

Birth `rotation`, `angularVelocity`, and `angularAcceleration`, plus the corresponding rotation-module options,
accept `Vector3Input`: a scalar or a `THREE.Vector3`. As with scale, a scalar expands uniformly across X, Y and Z.
Billboard sprites use X for their screen-space roll, so a scalar is sufficient. Meshes and non-billboard sprites
still use all three axes; supply an explicit vector for axis-specific rotation.

```ts
new Emitter({ initialValues: {
  rotation: [0, Math.PI * 2],
  angularVelocity: 0.65,
} });
new RotationOverLifetime({ angularVelocity: new Set([-1.8, 1.8]) });
new RotationBySpeed({ speedRange: [0, 10], angularVelocity: [0, 2] });
```

Angles use radians, angular velocity uses radians per second, and angular acceleration uses radians per second
squared. Lifetime options support constants, ranges, sets and callbacks, on CPU and GPU. Size, speed and depth options
retain their `ValueByParameter` semantics: ranges interpolate, direct values scale with the normalized parameter,
and callbacks supply explicit results. The particle's stored angular channels remain `THREE.Vector3` objects.

The [curves](https://www.npmjs.com/package/curves) package was designed and
built to streamline functional values by defining and evaluating eased curves,
similar to Unity's AnimationCurves with modifiers akin to Blender's FCurve
Modifiers. It has prebuilt keyframe types for numbers, colors, and vectors,
compatible with the `THREE.Vector3` and `THREE.Color` types.


## Parameter-Based Values

Depth, size, and speed modules use `ValueByParameter<T>` rather than random dynamic ranges.
A two-element array interpolates between its endpoints using the normalized parameter.
A direct numeric or vector value scales with that parameter; a function returns its explicit
result. For example, `[0.5, 2]` interpolates from 0.5 to 2, while `() => 2` supplies a constant
result. Check the option's actual type before assuming an array means random sampling.

Random lifetime values are often evaluated with a particle ID seed, so a particle keeps
its sampled choice across repeated module updates. Emitter birth sampling selects new
values for new particles. Do not mutate a vector supplied as a shared option inside a
custom callback; update the particle's own state or reuse a separate scratch vector.

GPU built-ins support the same constant, range, set, and callback forms. Function values are
sampled into an interpolated lookup table with `ParticleSystem.GPU_DYNAMIC_VALUE_RESOLUTION`
entries, so sharp or high-frequency curves may need a higher resolution. GPU-aware options can
also accept TSL nodes. Runtime value changes synchronize automatically; a change that alters a
custom shader graph's structure should additionally set that component's `needsUpdate` flag.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/emission-sources-events.md -->

# Emission Sources and Custom Events

A subsystem can follow a simulated particle or a persistent CPU-managed emission source. Registered sources use the
existing emitter contexts, tag intersection, deterministic ratio selection, numeric inheritance and event runs. They do
not enter the particle population, consume simulated slots, or require placeholder particles. Update only the owning
root system; its children share its clock.

## Registering and Updating Sources

```ts
const source = system.registerEmissionSource({
  tags: ['acid-pool'],
  transform: new THREE.Matrix4().makeTranslation(0, 0.1, 0),
  color: new THREE.Color('#78e832'),
  alpha: 1,
  scale: 1,
  velocity: new THREE.Vector3(),
  mass: 1,
});

source.update({ alpha: 0.5 });
source.emitEvent('bubble', { strength: 2 });
// Equivalent system methods:
system.updateSource(source.id, { alpha: 0.5 });
system.emitEvent(source.id, 'bubble', { strength: 2 });
// Use either removal form:
source.dispose();
system.unregisterEmissionSource(source.id);
```

Registration returns a `RegisteredEmissionSource` handle. The package already exports an `EmissionSource` enum for
geometry sampling (`Volume`, `Surface`, `Vertices`); that existing export remains compatible. The handle delegates
update, dispatch and disposal to its owning system and exposes `id`, `system`, canonical attributes, and a copied `data`
snapshot. Input matrices, vectors, colors and tag arrays are copied. Registered IDs start with `source:`; existing
particle IDs retain their format.

Transforms and velocities use the owning system's simulation space. In world simulation supply world transforms; in
Local or Source simulation premultiply world transforms by `getSimulationToWorldMatrix().invert()`.
The same conversion applies to Transform mode using its selected reference frame. The emitter's local +Y axis is the
outward axis for surface emission. Source transform scale and optional scalar `scale` combine for transform inheritance.
Updating attributes preserves identity, registration age, distance credit and burst progression.

A source remains alive until disposed or its owner is destroyed. Registration dispatches `spawn`; removal dispatches
`death` exactly once and immediately stops continuous emission. Repeated disposal is safe. Removal releases continuous
emitter context state; already created child particles and captured event runs finish normally. Ordinary particle
clearing does not remove externally registered sources; explicit removal or system destruction does.

`realtime` is source age in milliseconds of parent simulation time, respecting pause and simulation speed. `time` is
that age divided by the owning system duration. Registered sources have no finite particle lifetime; their child
emitters use their own duration and looping behavior. Set `inheritLifetime: 0` explicitly to communicate that
independent timing. `rateOverDistance` follows source transform movement using the same per-context distance accumulator
as particle-backed emission. Multiple position updates before one frame contribute the final displacement, rather than
every intermediate point.

## Selecting Sources and Inheriting Attributes

```ts
system.addSubSystem(smoke, {
  tags: ['acid-pool'],
  emitContinuous: true,
  ratio: 0.75,
  shouldEmit: source => source.alpha > 0.05,
  inheritLifetime: 0,
  inheritScale: 0.5,
  inheritColor: 1,
  inheritAlpha: 1,
  inheritVelocity: 0.25,
});
```

`tags` uses the same intersection semantics as modules and renderers: omission accepts every source; an empty selection
accepts none. Both particles and registered sources can drive this child simultaneously when their tags match. No
source-type switch is needed. `ratio` chooses sources consistently by identity; `shouldEmit` receives their common
attributes. Function-valued selectors use CPU evaluation; they cannot automatically become a native GPU predicate.
Native GPU particle consumers require boolean `shouldEmit`. Continuous CPU consumers of GPU particles receive
asynchronous snapshots through the existing selective readback infrastructure; their source contexts are released when
those snapshots report removal. Registered sources remain directly available to these selectors without source readback.

Inheritance factors remain numbers. Color, alpha, mass, and transform scale blend from neutral values using their
configured factors; inherited velocity adds the selected fraction of source velocity. Scale inheritance affects the
emission frame, while an event context's scalar `scale` multiplies child particle size. Child particles can themselves
drive nested subsystems, on CPU or GPU. Registered source updates do not restart continuous bursts or event runs.

## Event Origins and Defaults

`EventScope` selects event producers explicitly. Every selection is exclusive:

| Scope | Producers |
| --- | --- |
| `'local'` | The receiver's own system |
| `'parent'` | Its immediate parent only |
| `'child'` | Its immediate children only |
| `['local', 'parent']` | Its own system and immediate parent |
| `['local', 'parent', 'child']` | All three immediate origins |
| `[]` | None |

There is no recursive ancestor or descendant visibility, and repeated selections do not duplicate events.
Modules and renderers default to `'local'`. Root emitters default to `'local'`; subsystem emitters default to
`'parent'` only. These rules apply equally to lifecycle and custom events. A child emitter with `emitOnDeath: true`
therefore responds to parent deaths without restarting when its own particles die. Selecting `'local'` explicitly
allows local lifecycle reactions, including self-emission; use that intentionally.

Scope filters subscriptions. It does not forward events: a child observing parent events does not publish its own
events upward. Each delivered event preserves its original producer in `event.origin`, its identity, and its optional
source. GPU filtering checks producer identity and that producer's event-name mapping together; numeric event IDs
alone do not identify events across systems.

```ts
const emitter = new Emitter({
  eventScope: ['local', 'parent'],
  emitOnDeath: true,
  bursts: { time: 0, count: 8 },
});

// An explicit relationship scope replaces the emitter's selection for this attachment.
parent.addSubSystem(child, { eventScope: 'parent' });
```

Omitting the attachment override preserves an explicitly configured emitter scope, otherwise the subsystem default
applies. Attachment overrides never mutate the emitter, and detaching or reparenting discards the previous override.
The former cumulative `'both'` alias is replaced by explicit origin arrays in this major release.

Source tags select which origins may emit. They are not automatically copied to emitted particles: configure the
child emitter's own `tags` to label its output. For example, a rocket emitter can assign `['rocket']` and a sparkle
emitter can select `sourceTags: ['rocket']` while assigning `tags: ['sparkle']`. The same rule applies to registered
sources, continuous emission, and event bursts on CPU and GPU. Source identity and Source-space attachment do not
depend on tags.

## One Event API

```ts
system.emitEvent('alarm', { strength: 3 }); // No particle or transform is required.
system.emitEvent(particle.id, 'explode', { strength: 3 });
particle.emitEvent('explode', { strength: 3 });
source.emitEvent('bubble', { strength: 1.5 });

system.addSubSystem(splash, { onEvent: ['explode', 'bubble'] });
```

With an ID, `emitEvent` resolves a live particle or registered source in its owning system. Unknown or disposed IDs
are ignored. A CPU particle's alias uses ownership stored outside its serializable attributes. Cloning or making a
render-only shallow view does not copy that ownership. Dispatch never performs shader compilation or requires
explicit event registration.

CPU dispatch targeting a native GPU particle ID queues a generation-validated selective snapshot at
the next system update. Its CPU handler runs asynchronously when that snapshot is available, then
stages births for GPU children where appropriate. A recycled or dead generation is ignored. Calls
are batched without coalescing separate events, and a busy readback pool retries the batch. This
explicit CPU-to-GPU targeting is separate from GPU-native events, which need no snapshot readback.

An event-only subscription disables continuous emission by default. Set `emitContinuous: true` when both are desired.
`emitOnSpawn`, `emitOnDeath` and `emitOnCollision` remain supported; subscribing to a built-in event through both a
legacy flag and `onEvent` creates one run, with the named callback applied once. Explicit collision events can also
originate from registered sources. Supplying the established collision hit shape preserves impulse threshold, alignment
and scaling behavior.

### Declarative Consumers

`Module`, `Renderer`, and `Emitter` extend `EventReceiver`. The superclass owns their `events` and
`eventScope` subscriptions, CPU and GPU execution contexts, batching, overflow tracking, and subscription cleanup.
Components extend the shared execution context when needed; modules add access to their managed octree.
CPU execution contexts expose a read-only `events` batch. Module `prepare(context)`, conditions, and particle callbacks
share one execution context, so shared event interpretation can happen once during preparation. Native GPU modules
use `context.events.forEach(name, callback)` over shared storage without event readback.

Events emitted during consumption remain pending for a subsequent eligible execution. CPU receivers retain the newest
1024 pending events and count dropped oldest entries in `overflowCount`. GPU receivers keep independent
cursors into bounded shared storage; entries overwritten before a receiver executes are dropped. A receiver that does
not execute retains pending events until its next execution, subject to these bounds.

`system.onEvent(nameOrNames, callback)` observes only events produced by that system and returns an unsubscribe
function. Declarative scopes subscribe to the relevant producer dispatchers directly; they do not rebroadcast events.

### CPU Context Handlers

```ts
system.addSubSystem(splash, {
  tags: ['acid-pool'],
  onEvent: {
    bubble: (data, source, context) => {
      if (typeof data !== 'object' || data === null
        || !('strength' in data) || typeof data.strength !== 'number') return;
      return {
        scale: context.scale * data.strength,
        velocity: context.velocity.clone().add(new THREE.Vector3(0, data.strength, 0)),
      };
    },
  },
});
```

CPU handlers execute immediately at dispatch, receive an arbitrary JavaScript payload typed as `unknown`, a common
source view, and the inherited `EmissionContext`, and may return partial overrides. Applications narrow or assert their
own payload schema; the library never needs to know it. Event contexts own their mutable values. Changing an event
context never changes persistent source attributes. A run captures the resolved values, so later source updates or
disposal do not alter that event.

Context overrides include transform, position, color, alpha, mass, velocity, scalar scale, velocityScale,
distortionStrength and duration. Identity and elapsed run timing remain owned by the scheduler. A position-only override
updates transform translation; a transform-only override updates the context position. Supplying both keeps both
explicit values. Collision runs retain existing impulse effects and their snapshot-based lifecycle.

## GPU-Native Events

Inside a module's `modifyGPU(particle, deltaTime, context)`, use `particle.emitEvent(name, payload)` within the relevant
TSL control flow. It appends a snapshot and payload to the existing GPU event buffer at that point in the graph.
Multiple events from one particle remain separate records.

```ts
system.addSubSystem(splash, {
  onEvent: {
    explode: (data, source, context) => {
      if (typeof data !== 'object' || data === null
        || !('strength' in data) || typeof data.strength !== 'number') return;
      return { scale: context.scale * data.strength };
    },
    gpu: {
      explode: (data, particle, context) => ({
        scale: context.scale.mul(data[0].x),
        velocity: context.velocity.add(particle.velocity.mul(data[0].y)),
      }),
    },
  },
});
```

GPU handlers are JavaScript callbacks that **build TSL expressions during kernel compilation**. They are not JavaScript
callbacks executed per particle or per event at runtime. Return TSL nodes for context overrides. GPU context includes
`transform` (a matrix node), `position`, `color`, `alpha`, `mass`, `velocity`, `scale`, `velocityScale`, and `duration`;
transform and position overrides use the same translation precedence as CPU contexts. Full affine transforms are
preserved in persistent GPU event runs.

Names are discovered automatically from both CPU and GPU subscriptions. Built-in IDs remain death = 1, spawn = 2,
collision = 3. Each parent system supports **32 distinct names: three built-ins plus 29 custom names**. IDs are retained
for that system's lifetime, including previously used names after a subscription is removed. Exceeding capacity throws a
diagnostic. Subscription changes can rebuild the affected GPU kernels; data updates and dispatch do not.

An unsubscribed GPU event name produces no record. If both implementations exist, GPU-origin events use the GPU handler
and CPU-origin events use the CPU handler. A GPU-origin event with only a CPU handler is delivered asynchronously
through event readback. Array subscriptions and `true` entries need no handler and can stay GPU-native.

## GPU Payload Format and Capacity

Each GPU event accepts either one `vec4` node or an array with one to three `vec4` nodes:

```ts
particle.emitEvent('explode', vec4(strength, 0, 0, 0));
particle.emitEvent('impact', [vec4(position, 0), vec4(normal, 0), vec4(impulse, 0)]);
```

The maximum is **three vec4 values, or twelve float components per record**. A fourth vector produces a development-time
error during graph construction. Missing vectors are explicitly initialized to zero, including built-in events that do
not use payloads. Every GPU handler receives exactly three entries, accessible as `data[0]`, `data[1]`, and `data[2]`.
Each supports `.x`, `.y`, `.z`, `.w` and vector swizzles such as `.xyz`.

Payloads contain numerical TSL values. Arbitrary JavaScript objects cannot be sent through a native GPU event. The
particle snapshot is stored separately and remains available to the handler even after the original particle dies or its
slot is reused. Identity validation retains the original slot generation; readback never substitutes the particle
currently occupying that slot.

The event record remains **15 vec4 slots**. Its existing collision point, normal and impulse slots are generalized as
Payload0, Payload1 and Payload2. For collisions, their `.xyz` retain point, normal and impulse, with `.w = 0`. The
separate per-particle collision cache and existing collision APIs remain intact. No additional event buffer or storage
binding is needed for custom payloads.

### Example A: One Scalar

```ts
// Inside modifyGPU:
particle.emitEvent('explode', vec4(strength, 0, 0, 0));
// Inside onEvent.gpu:
const explode = (data, particle, context) => ({
  scale: context.scale.mul(data[0].x),
});
```

Here `data[0].x` carries strength; `data[1]` and `data[2]` are zero vectors.

### Example B: Multiple Parameters

```ts
particle.emitEvent('explode', vec4(strength, radius, temperature, 0));
const explode = (data, particle, context) => ({
  scale: context.scale.mul(data[0].x),
  position: context.position.add(vec3(0, data[0].y, 0)),
  alpha: context.alpha.mul(data[0].z.div(200).clamp(0, 1)),
});
```

This application chooses `.x` for strength, `.y` for radius, `.z` for temperature and leaves `.w` unused. These semantic
meanings are conventions chosen by the developer; RZMPS does not assign them.

### Example C: All Three Vectors

```ts
particle.emitEvent('impact', [
  vec4(position, 0),
  vec4(normal, 0),
  vec4(impulse, 0),
]);
const impact = (data, particle, context) => ({
  position: data[0].xyz,
  velocity: context.velocity.add(data[1].xyz.mul(data[2].xyz.length())),
  scale: context.scale.mul(data[2].xyz.length().max(0.1)),
});
```

This custom impact convention uses position, normal and impulse, reading every vector. It is independent of the built-in
collision event. [Fireflies](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireflies.html) uses a smaller payload for a neighbor-driven light pulse;
applications only need to fill the components their child effect consumes.

### Readback Representation

GPU events delivered to CPU custom handlers carry `readonly [THREE.Vector4, THREE.Vector4, THREE.Vector4]`. The array
contains decoded numerical values from the event snapshot, not an invented object schema. For example, use `data[0].x`
on CPU too. CPU-generated events may instead carry arbitrary JavaScript data, such as `{ strength: 2 }`. These payload
representations are intentionally different. A CPU callback serving both origins should discriminate the payload shape.

Built-in collision listeners retain their established `CollisionHit` interface. Custom named GPU callbacks receive the
numerical three-vector payload. GPU-to-CPU delivery is asynchronous and preserves frame delivery order as provided by
the existing event pipeline. It may arrive after the originating particle dies; the captured snapshot remains valid for
that run.

## Synchronization and Performance

Registered sources are CPU-managed. Calls to `source.update()` only change canonical CPU attributes; repeated calls
coalesce automatically. At the next system update, existing emitter contexts evaluate continuous and event-run births,
then GPU children receive a single reusable batch. GPU allocation chooses actual free destination slots. No per-source
compute dispatch, source readback or shader recompilation occurs. Applications do not need to throttle updates manually.
This implementation evaluates registered-source emitter scheduling on CPU even when child particle simulation runs on
GPU.

Event dispatches are never coalesced with attribute updates. Every dispatch captures its own context. Persistent event
runs and continuous distance/rate credits retain their separate identities and are released at completion or source
removal. GPU upload storage grows geometrically and is reused across frames.

GPU-generated events consumed entirely by native GPU subsystems use the existing GPU event stream without event-buffer
CPU readback. CPU listeners, CPU-only predicates or CPU event handlers can require asynchronous delivery. Ordinary
particle and allocation diagnostics have their own independent readback behavior.

Three separate limits matter: distinct event names (32), floats per payload (12), and records in the shared event buffer
per frame (`ParticleSystem.GPU_EVENT_BUFFER_CAPACITY`). Custom events share capacity with spawn, death and collision
records. Overflow bounds-checks writes, discards excess records and increments the existing overflow diagnostic.
Concurrent persistent runs also have a finite destination capacity; size child `maxParticles` and event capacity for the
intended overlap. CPU-staged births obey child particle capacity and available GPU slots. Very dense events can be
dropped safely when those destinations are full.

## Persistent Decals

```ts
const decals = new DecalRenderer(material, {
  onSpawn: false,
  onCollision: true,
  emissionTags: ['acid-pool'],
  lifetime: 18,
});
// Attach decals as a renderer of system before emitting particles.
system.addRenderer(decals);
system.addSubSystem(smoke, { tags: ['acid-pool'], emitContinuous: true, inheritLifetime: 0 });
system.addSubSystem(splash, { tags: ['acid-pool'], onEvent: ['bubble'], inheritLifetime: 0 });
for (const decal of decals.decals) {
  decal.source?.emitEvent('bubble', { strength: 0.5 + Math.random() });
}
```

Only decals with `emissionTags` register sources. `decal.source` exposes the persistent handle; its transform uses the
actual decal footprint and points +Y along the outward surface normal. Color and alpha follow the decal material. Moving
rigid surfaces update emission frames automatically. Expiry, eviction, clear/reset and renderer destruction dispose
handles and dispatch death before releasing contexts. Already emitted children remain alive. See [Surface
Decals](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/decals.html) and the complete [Acid](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/acid.html) factory for independent randomized bubbling and
fading smoke.


Use [Source simulation space](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/subsystems.html#simulation-frames) when emitted particles should remain attached to their
origin as it moves, rotates, or scales. Ordinary Local/World subsystem emission samples the origin at birth; Source
space retains the live source relationship for the child's lifetime.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/first-gpu-module.md -->

# First GPU Module

A custom module needs a CPU callback and a TSL callback to behave on both simulation backends.
This example adds the same upward acceleration in each path.

```ts
import { Module, ParticleSystem } from "@rzmps/rzmps";
import { float, vec3 } from "three/tsl";

const updraft = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime) => {
    particle.velocity.y += 0.5 * deltaTime;
  },
  {
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime) => {
      const acceleration = vec3(0, float(0.5).mul(deltaTime), 0);
      particle.velocity.assign(particle.velocity.add(acceleration));
    },
  },
);

const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters,
  modules: [updraft],
  renderers,
  gpuProcessing: true,
});
```

The CPU callback runs once for each JavaScript particle. The GPU callback runs while RZMPS builds
a compute graph: its particle properties and `deltaTime` are TSL nodes, not current JavaScript
values. Build expressions with TSL functions and write fields with `assign`; JavaScript arithmetic
or branching cannot inspect a node's per-particle value.

The two callbacks should express the same behavior, but they need not use identical algorithms.
`supportsGPU` is true only when `modifyGPU` exists and every custom CPU condition has a matching
`conditionGPU`. After the renderer initializes, use `particles.isGPUProcessingActive` to check the
backend actually selected.

## Conditions and Spatial Queries

A custom CPU `condition` also needs a TSL equivalent:

```ts
const risingOnly = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime) => {
    particle.velocity.y += 0.5 * deltaTime;
  },
  {
    condition: (particle) => particle.velocity.y > 0,
    conditionGPU: (particle) => particle.velocity.y.greaterThan(0),
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime) => {
      particle.velocity.y.addAssign(float(0.5).mul(deltaTime));
    },
  },
);
```

## Managed Spatial Grid

The GPU counterpart to a managed octree is `ParticleSpatialGrid`. This version of the crowd-drag
module uses the grid's exact-radius query and performs the count entirely in the compute graph:

```ts
const crowdDrag = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime, { octree }) => {
    const nearbyCount = octree
      .particlesInRadius(particle.position, 2)
      .filter((neighbor) => neighbor !== particle)
      .length;
    particle.velocity.multiplyScalar(
      Math.max(0, 1 - nearbyCount * 0.02 * deltaTime),
    );
  },
  {
    useOctree: true,
    octreeOptions: { maxDepth: 6, particlesPerLeaf: 8 },
    useSpatialGrid: true,
    spatialGridOptions: { brickSubdivisions: 3, cellSubdivisions: 4 },
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime, { spatialGrid: grid }) => {
      if (!grid) return;

      const nearbyCount = float(0).toVar("nearbyCount");
      grid.forEachParticleInRadius(
        particle.position,
        float(2),
        () => nearbyCount.addAssign(1),
        { excludeIndex: particle.index },
      );
      const damping = float(1)
        .sub(nearbyCount.mul(0.02).mul(deltaTime))
        .max(0);
      particle.velocity.mulAssign(damping);
    },
  },
);
```

RZMPS rebuilds both structures and exposes them as `context.octree` on CPU and `context.spatialGrid` on GPU. A
grid query emits shader-side work and never returns JavaScript particles. Its callback can inspect
each neighbor and the squared distance when a count alone is not enough. Keep query bounds and
grid resolution appropriate for the effect; see
[particle spatial acceleration](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/particle-octree.html) for configuration and limitations.

Runtime scalar, vector, color, range, and curve properties on built-in modules synchronize to GPU
parameters automatically. A custom class can use its protected `gpuParameters` store for the same
pattern. Set `needsUpdate = true` only when a change alters graph structure or owned resources.

## Killing a Particle

Call `particle.kill()` on either backend. For a permanent boundary rule, pair a CPU condition with a TSL condition:

```ts
const boundary = new Module(
  particle => {
    if (particle.position.y < -10) particle.kill();
  },
  {
    modifyGPU(particle) {
      If(particle.position.y.lessThan(-10), () => {
        particle.kill();
      });
    },
  },
);
```

`If` comes from `three/tsl`. The default module priority is permanent. The GPU helper marks the slot dead immediately
and advances its age past its lifetime using finite values. Normal death-event subscribers still receive one event,
including when the module runs in a separate stored update before integration. Event source snapshots are historical
views and cannot kill a live particle.

The [Fireflies example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireflies.html) kills insects outside its volume instead of steering them toward
boundaries, and replenishes them through ordinary emission to maintain a roaming population with a bounded spatial grid.

Continue with [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) for execution phases, fallback rules, readback,
and validation.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/first-gpu-spatial-effect.md -->

# First GPU Spatial Effect

A custom spatial effect pairs its ordinary particle modifier with `modifyGPU`. Built-in volume
factories provide the CPU inclusion test and GPU influence calculation automatically.

```ts
import { ParticleSystem, SpatialEffect } from "@rzmps/rzmps";
import { float, vec3 } from "three/tsl";

const updraft = SpatialEffect.Sphere(
  (particle, deltaTime, _system, strength) => {
    particle.velocity.y += 2 * deltaTime * strength;
  },
  {
    automaticFeather: false,
    feather: 0.75,
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime, _context, strength) => {
      const acceleration = vec3(0, float(2).mul(deltaTime).mul(strength), 0);
      particle.velocity.assign(particle.velocity.add(acceleration));
    },
  },
  2,
  24,
  16,
);

updraft.position.set(0, 1, 0);
scene.add(updraft);

const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters,
  modules,
  renderers,
  gpuProcessing: true,
});
scene.add(particles);
```

With `automaticFeather: false`, both callbacks receive a strength from zero through one, so the
example applies feathering explicitly and identically. With automatic feathering enabled, RZMPS
blends supported particle fields around the callback instead.

`SpatialEffect.Sphere`, `Box`, `Cone`, and `Torus` supply matching built-in CPU and GPU tests. Add
`conditionGPU` only when adding a custom CPU `condition`. Add `testGPU` when replacing the volume's
inclusion rule with a custom `test`; it returns a float influence rather than a JavaScript boolean.
Custom geometry without `testGPU` uses a baked influence field.

Spatial effects are scene objects. Their transforms can move while
`updatePolicy: SpatialEffectUpdatePolicy.TransformDynamic` updates transform data without
rebuilding geometry acceleration. Use `GeometryDynamic` only when vertex data itself changes.
Custom tests are not bounds-filtered because RZMPS cannot assume they depend on the effect's
geometry.

After the renderer initializes, verify `particles.isGPUProcessingActive`. Unsupported generic
spatial effects are skipped by GPU simulation instead of forcing the entire system onto CPU, so
also inspect each custom effect's `supportsGPU` while developing it. See
[GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) for batching, invalidation, and profiling.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/first-module.md -->

# First Module

Modules change particle values over time. A custom module receives the live
particle, the frame delta, and a shared execution context.

```ts
import { Module } from "@rzmps/rzmps";

const riseAndFade = new Module((particle, deltaTime) => {
  particle.velocity.y += 0.5 * deltaTime;
  particle.alpha *= 1 - particle.time;
});
```

Attach it to a system with the rest of your modules:

```ts
const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters,
  modules: [riseAndFade],
  renderers,
});
```

Use `condition` when only some particles should be affected:

```ts
const sparksOnly = new Module((particle) => {
  particle.scale.multiplyScalar(1.2);
}, {
  condition: (particle) => particle.tags?.includes("spark") ?? false,
});
```

The exported `ModuleCondition` type receives the same arguments as `ModuleUpdate`:
`(particle, deltaTime, context)`, and returns a boolean. The context exposes the owning `system`,
`deltaTime`, a read-only `events` batch, and the optional managed `octree`. Preparation, conditions,
and particle callbacks share one context for the execution. Conditions run after alive and tag
filtering. Callbacks can omit arguments they do not need. On GPU, `ModuleGPUCondition` matches
`ModuleGPUUpdate`'s arguments and returns a TSL boolean node; its context exposes the managed
`spatialGrid` and native event batch.

This major release replaces the former `(particle, deltaTime, system?, octree?)` signature.
Move system and spatial queries into the context; class preparation now receives `prepare(context)`.
There is one callback path for both function-defined and class-based modules.

Declare `events` and optionally `eventScope` in module options to receive subscribed events. Modules default to
`'local'`; use `'parent'` for the immediate parent only, or an array such as `['local', 'parent']` to combine origins.
The batch is frozen before preparation and stays the same through conditions and particle updates.
Events emitted during those callbacks remain pending until a subsequent execution. Use the preparation
hook to interpret a batch once when the result can be shared across particles.

For performance-sensitive modules, avoid allocating objects inside the per
particle callback. Reuse vectors and colors outside the callback when possible.

A plain Module defaults to permanent priority. The example's velocity increment accumulates over time; multiplying by
delta seconds makes 0.5 an acceleration rather than an amount per frame. Its alpha multiplication also accumulates. For
a fade defined entirely by normalized age, prefer ColorOverLifetime or set `priority: Module.Priority.Transient` so the
fade is reapplied to cached base alpha each frame.

Use `Module.Priority.PreMovementTransient` when a temporary velocity adjustment must affect this frame's integration.
Render-time transient modules run after movement. See [module priority](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/module-priority.html) before combining several
modules that assign the same property.

## System Update Hooks

`prepare(context)` can also run effect-level scheduling once per simulation step, even when a module does
not modify individual particles. Supply an empty CPU callback and `modifyGPU() {}` to keep both backends supported,
then put the shared scheduling work in `prepare(context)`. Read `context.system` and `context.deltaTime` there. Call
`super.prepare(context)` to preserve the base preparation behavior.
Function-defined modules can supply the same hook as an option:

```ts
const scheduler = new Module(() => {}, {
  prepare({ system, deltaTime }) {
    // Advance application scheduling on the simulation clock.
    advanceSchedule(system, deltaTime);
  },
  modifyGPU() {},
});
```

This follows the system's pause state, simulation speed and fixed-step advancement.

[Acid](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/acid.html) uses this pattern to schedule independent bubble events from persistent decal sources.
Its per-particle callbacks intentionally do nothing. The demo factory returns a ParticleSystem, so this hook lets it
keep scheduling on the system's clock without owning an animation loop. Applications with their own animation loop
can instead schedule events there before calling the root system's update().

## Managed Octree

Particle-to-particle comparisons should use a managed `ParticleOctree` instead of scanning the
whole particle array for every particle. Enable it in the module options; RZMPS rebuilds it and
exposes it through `context.octree` in preparation, conditions, and particle callbacks.

```ts
const crowdDrag = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime, { octree }) => {
    const nearbyCount = octree
      .particlesInRadius(particle.position, 2)
      .filter((neighbor) => neighbor !== particle)
      .length;
    const damping = Math.max(0, 1 - nearbyCount * 0.02 * deltaTime);
    particle.velocity.multiplyScalar(damping);
  },
  {
    useOctree: true,
    octreeOptions: {
      maxDepth: 6,
      particlesPerLeaf: 8,
    },
  },
);
```

The octree prunes nodes outside the query sphere, then returns the particles that pass exact
distance checks in the remaining leaves. Custom aggregate data remains useful when an
approximation such as average position or velocity is cheaper than collecting every matching
particle; see
[particle spatial acceleration](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/particle-octree.html).

For reusable behavior, extend Module and pass your per-particle callback and options to `super`. Override
`prepare(context)` when expensive shared work should happen once per frame; call `super.prepare` if using
automatic spatial-effect collection. Put resource cleanup in `cleanup()`. Dependencies in `dependents` participate in
normal priority sorting rather than forcing an independent update loop.

Built-in modules already cover forces, noise, scale, rotation, depth, color, and collision. Reuse those when their
semantics match the effect. Custom callbacks are most useful for application-specific logic, and should mutate the
particle provided rather than storing a shared mutable vector in multiple particles.

The callback above is CPU-only. Continue with [First GPU Module](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-module.html) to add the
equivalent TSL operation, then use [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) as the reference for managed
spatial queries, invalidation, and testing requirements.

# First Spatial Effect

Spatial effects modify particles based on scene-space volumes or custom tests.
Use a built-in force field when particles should react to an area in the scene.

```ts
import * as THREE from "three";
import { ParticleForceField } from "@rzmps/rzmps";

const updraft = ParticleForceField.Sphere({
  direction: new THREE.Vector3(0, 2, 0),
}, 2);

updraft.position.set(0, 1, 0);
scene.add(updraft);
```

Particle systems discover generic spatial effects in their scene by default.
Disable that behavior per system with `useSpatialEffects: false`, or use
`spatialEffectFilter` to choose which effects apply.

```ts
const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  spatialEffectFilter: (effect) => effect.name === "updraft",
});
```

Use `KillZone` when particles should be removed inside a volume:

```ts
import { KillZone } from "@rzmps/rzmps";

const cleanup = KillZone.Box(10, 4, 10);
cleanup.position.y = -3;
scene.add(cleanup);
```

Name the updraft (`updraft.name = 'updraft'`) before using the filter shown above. A filter cannot find an unnamed field by that name. The direction vector supplies acceleration while the field applies its timestep. In custom callbacks, multiply acceleration by deltaTime before adding it to velocity.

For a custom volume modifier, use `SpatialEffect.Box((particle, deltaTime) => { ... }, options, width, height, depth)`. Scale and position it like another Object3D. A custom `test` option can replace the geometric inclusion rule, while `inverted` applies to the opposite side of a volume. Choose a permanent priority for forces and a transient priority for temporary color or scale changes.

Scene discovery and module-level collections serve different purposes. A generic field modifies intersecting particles directly; a specialized affector can instead be collected by a module such as Boids. See [spatial collections](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/spatial-effects.html) for explicit selection and filtering, and [module priority](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/module-priority.html) for execution phases.

Custom CPU callbacks do not translate into shader code. Continue with
[First GPU Spatial Effect](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-spatial-effect.html) to pair this volume with a TSL modifier,
then use [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) as the reference for batching and moving-geometry
policies.
