<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/gpu-processing.md -->

# GPU Processing and Extension Development

RZMPS keeps the same `ParticleSystem` composition on CPU and GPU: emitters create particles,
modules and spatial effects modify them, and renderers display them. Set `gpuProcessing: true`
(the default) and render the system once with an initialized Three.js `WebGPURenderer` to make
GPU simulation eligible. `isGPUProcessingActive` reports the backend actually selected for the
current system; `gpuProcessing` only expresses the requested mode.

```ts
const particles = new ParticleSystem({
  emitters: [emitter],
  modules: [force, color],
  renderers: [sprites],
  gpuProcessing: true,
});

scene.add(particles);
renderer.setAnimationLoop(() => {
  particles.update();
  renderer.render(scene, camera);
});
```

WebGL always uses CPU simulation. A WebGPU system also uses CPU simulation when GPU processing is
disabled, a module lacks a GPU implementation, GPU tag capacity is exceeded, or a CPU-input
renderer is combined with a render-time modifier. Unsupported generic spatial effects are skipped
by the GPU path rather than moving the entire system to CPU. Inspect `supportsGPU`,
`getGPUEmissionSupport()`, `getGPUExecutionSchedule()`, and `isGPUProcessingActive` when composing
custom components. Changing `gpuProcessing` starts a fresh run because CPU objects and GPU buffers
are separate authoritative states.

## Writing CPU and GPU Modules

The CPU callback mutates a JavaScript `Particle`. `modifyGPU` builds a Three.js Shading Language
(TSL) graph over a `GPUParticleLike`; it does not execute once per particle in JavaScript. Work
through [First GPU Module](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-module.html) for a complete paired implementation and
[First GPU Spatial Effect](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-gpu-spatial-effect.html) for influence, feathering, and custom test
rules.

Reuse ordinary CPU hooks for setup and cleanup. `prepare(context)` runs once before a
module's work on either backend. A function-defined module can request managed acceleration with
`useOctree`/`octreeOptions` for CPU or `useSpatialGrid`/`spatialGridOptions` for GPU; the resulting
`ParticleOctree` is available as `context.octree` on CPU; the GPU context exposes `context.spatialGrid`.
Both callbacks use `(particle, deltaTime, context)`, as do their conditions.
`cleanup()` must call `super.cleanup()` when overridden so managed references are released.

Dynamic numbers, vectors, colors, ranges, sets, and callbacks are available to built-in GPU
components. Callback curves are sampled into interpolated uniform tables at
`ParticleSystem.GPU_DYNAMIC_VALUE_RESOLUTION`; increase it when a high-frequency curve needs more
fidelity. TSL nodes can be supplied directly where a dynamic value is evaluated by GPU code.

## Emitters and Spatial Effects

Built-in GPU emission supports rate, distance rate, timed bursts, tags, initial values, LOD, and
volume, surface, or vertex sampling from buffer geometry. CPU and GPU volume emission share the
shape's baked Halton sample table. `volumeSamples` is `"auto"` by default; assigning a number fixes
the table size, while changing geometry or the sample setting rebuilds it. Surface selection is
weighted by triangle area. Burst times are normalized emission-cycle values from 0 through 1.

Emitters use the built-in GPU birth pipeline; they are configured through `Emitter` and
`EmissionShape`, not extended with a separate shader callback. Custom behavior belongs in a
module or spatial effect after birth.

Custom `SpatialEffect` implementations pair the CPU `modify`, `condition`, and `test` callbacks
with `modifyGPU`, `conditionGPU`, and `testGPU`. The GPU test returns a float influence from 0 to 1,
which supplies feather strength to `modifyGPU`. Built-in analytic volumes are batched and indexed.
Custom geometry uses a baked field, controlled by `bakedFieldResolution`; set `updatePolicy` to
`Static`, `TransformDynamic`, or `GeometryDynamic` when automatic change detection is not the best
fit. Custom tests are not bounds-filtered because RZMPS cannot assume they depend on geometry.

## Renderers, Events, and Readback

GPU-native renderers override `_updateGPU` and consume `GPUParticleBufferState` or the compact
render-output buffer. A renderer whose implementation needs ordinary `Particle` objects can
override `_updateGPU` and call the protected `updateCPUFromGPU` helper. It selectively reads the
requested fields, ignores overlapping requests while one is pending, and passes the resulting
particles through the renderer's public `update` method. Override `updateGPUUsesCPUReadback` to
keep child expansion on that CPU path:

```ts
class DebugRenderer extends Renderer {
  get updateGPUUsesCPUReadback() { return true; }

  _updateGPU(buffers, system, deltaTime) {
    this.updateCPUFromGPU(
      buffers,
      system,
      deltaTime,
      64,
      ["position", "color", "alpha"],
    );
  }

  _update(particles) {
    // Render the selectively reconstructed Particle objects.
  }
}
```

Request only the slots and fields the renderer actually consumes. Outside a renderer, use the
public system API directly:

```ts
const samples = await system.selectiveReadback(64, ["position", "color", "alpha"]);
```

Readback is delayed and may return no result if its bounded pool is busy. Do not use it to drive
same-frame simulation decisions. Lifecycle and collision events are also delivered asynchronously
from GPU buffers, so listeners and CPU audio/render views can lag simulation slightly. GPU-native
subsystems consume spawn, death, collision, and continuous emission on the GPU; update only the
root system, as on CPU.

Native subsystem births stay within WebGPU's default limit of eight compute-stage storage-buffer
bindings. Parent and child particle state each use separate float and integer buffers. The
remaining pass-specific bindings come from packed allocation state, the emitter-runtime fields
actually referenced by that pass, and packed shape-sampling data. Emitters dispatch separately so
adding emitters does not accumulate their geometry bindings in one shader. Applications do not
need to request a higher device limit.

## Collision and Neighbor Queries

`Collision` selects `ThreeCollisionBackend` for CPU processing and `ThreeGPUCollisionBackend` for
GPU processing when no backend is supplied. An explicit CPU-only backend makes the module GPU
incompatible. GPU collision does not support applying impulses back to scene bodies. Classify GPU
geometry with `CollisionGeometryUpdatePolicy`: static geometry is built once, transform-dynamic
geometry updates transforms, and geometry-dynamic meshes refit or rebuild changed acceleration
data.

Use `ParticleOctree` for CPU neighbor work and `ParticleSpatialGrid` for GPU queries. A grid query
emits TSL and invokes its visitor in shader code; it does not return JavaScript particles. Bounds
can expand automatically, but a larger volume lowers spatial resolution because the logical cell
count stays fixed. `maxQuerySteps: 0` performs unbounded exact traversal; a positive value is an
explicit performance cap.

## Configuration and Validation

Built-in components synchronize ordinary runtime property changes before each GPU frame. Constant
and sampled value changes update uniforms; structural changes invalidate and rebuild the affected
compute graph or resources. Custom components should expose changed scalar/vector data through
their GPU parameter nodes and set `needsUpdate = true` when changing graph structure, geometry
layout, callback identity, or buffer ownership.

Test both execution paths. WebGPU rendering alone does not prove GPU simulation is active: assert
`isGPUProcessingActive` after rendering has captured its context. Compare CPU and GPU behavior at
fixed timesteps, exercise resets and subsystem events, and inspect `gpuBufferStats`,
`gpuEventStats`, `gpuSpatialStats`, `gpuSelectiveReadbackStats`, and `gpuConfigurationStats` when
profiling. GPU output is expected to be behaviorally equivalent, not bit-for-bit identical.

See [renderer children and population LOD](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/renderer-children-lod.html) for system quality, destructive culling, visual expansion, hierarchy access, and default GPU buffer limits.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/module-priority.md -->

# Module Priority and Execution Order

RZMPS sorts modules and generic spatial effects together by numeric priority. Smaller priorities run first within a phase. Input order is preserved for equal priorities. A module's `dependents` are flattened before sorting; each dependent's own priority still determines its phase.

| Priority | Phase | Persistence |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Less than 0 | Before movement | Changes become permanent simulation state |
| 0 up to, excluding, 1 | Before movement | Transient changes influence this frame's movement |
| 1 or greater | After movement | Transient changes affect this frame's rendered appearance |

Use `Module.Priority.Permanent` (`-1`) for acceleration or accumulated changes. Multiply acceleration by `deltaTime` so the change is expressed per second. Use `Module.Priority.PreMovementTransient` (`0.5`) for a temporary velocity adjustment that should influence integration without accumulating into next frame's base velocity. Use `Module.Priority.Transient` (`1`) for a size or tint multiplier derived from normalized particle age.

At the beginning of the next update, cached values are restored. A render-time velocity change therefore does not move the particle in the current frame, and it does not automatically become next frame's velocity. This is why changing the priority can change the meaning of an otherwise identical callback.

Prefer a built-in lifetime module before writing an equivalent callback: those modules already select phases appropriate to their behavior. When combining modifiers that write the same property, inspect both their priorities and whether each callback assigns or multiplies that property. A later assignment can replace an earlier result.

`prepare(context)` runs before the per-particle phase. Use it for shared calculations or spatial collection, and reuse
scratch objects in the particle callback. Population LOD removes simulated particles before module work; surviving
particles run every step.

<!-- Source: apps/docs/guides/particle-octree.md -->

# Particle Spatial Acceleration

RZMPS provides complementary structures for particle-to-particle work:

| Operation | `ParticleOctree` (CPU) | `ParticleSpatialGrid` (GPU) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bounds | `setBounds`, `bounds` | `setBounds`, `bounds` |
| Resolution | `maxDepth`, `particlesPerLeaf` | `maxDepth`, brick/cell subdivisions |
| Update | `rebuild(particles, tags?)` | `rebuild(renderer, buffers, token?)` |
| Position lookup | `locate(position)` returns a node | `locate(position)` returns a cell coordinate |
| Radius query | `particlesInRadius` array | `forEachParticleInRadius` TSL visitor |
| Quality | `timeQuality` | `timeQuality` |
| Cleanup | garbage-collected CPU data | `dispose(renderer?)` / `destroy(renderer?)` |

Use `ParticleOctree` for CPU comparisons, neighborhood queries, and aggregate approximations. Use
`ParticleSpatialGrid` for GPU comparisons and exact-radius shader queries. They share conceptual
configuration names where the meanings match, but their results are intentionally different:
octree queries return CPU particle arrays and expose aggregates, while grid queries emit shader work and never
materialize a JavaScript particle array.

## CPU: ParticleOctree

`ParticleOctree<TAggregate>` groups particle positions into cubic cells and computes an application-defined aggregate. It supports exact-radius queries as well as aggregate approximations. It is separate from mesh collision acceleration: its entries are particle indices, not triangle faces.

Supply a configuration and an aggregator with `new` and `combine` functions. `new` must handle an absent particle because the tree asks it for an empty node aggregate. `combine` merges aggregates; return independent state or carefully manage mutation so sibling nodes cannot corrupt one another.

```ts
import { ParticleOctree } from '@rzmps/rzmps';

const tree = new ParticleOctree<number>({
  maxDepth: 6,
  particlesPerLeaf: 8,
  timeQuality: 1,
}, {
  new: (particle) => particle ? 1 : 0,
  combine: (a, b) => a + b,
});

tree.setBounds(system.boundingBox);
tree.rebuild(system.particles);
const node = tree.locate(system.particles[0].position);
const neighbors = tree.particlesInRadius(
  system.particles[0].position,
  2,
  { excludeIndex: 0 },
);
```

Guard the last line when the population is empty. `rebuild` accepts an optional tag selection. Only particles inside the resolved bounds and matching that selection contribute. Choose bounds in the same coordinate space as particle positions. Call `setBounds` when your population moves beyond the original volume; `locate` returns the root for a position outside the tree, which is not a nearest-neighbor result.

`maxDepth` defaults to 8 and `particlesPerLeaf` to 4. Deeper trees reduce cell size but increase node construction and neighbor bookkeeping. Increasing leaf capacity limits subdivision in dense populations. `timeQuality` defaults to 1; values below 1 skip some rebuilds after the first build. Check the boolean return from `rebuild` before assuming aggregates describe the current frame.

`particlesInRadius` prunes nodes using sphere-AABB intersection before exact distance tests in
leaf nodes. It is typically `O(log n + k)` for a balanced tree and `k` results, with an `O(n)`
worst case for broad queries or degenerate distributions. Options can exclude one particle index
and require matching tags. Queries use the population and node placement from the last successful
rebuild, so throttled trees may omit particles that have since crossed into the query volume.

`getNodes()` returns a new array of node references. Nodes expose bounds, neighbors, aggregate, and indices into the particle array passed to the last successful rebuild. Rebuilds replace node identities; do not retain nodes across rebuilds. Treat skipped rebuild data as stale if particles have been removed or reordered. `quantizeBounds` can stabilize moving bounds to reduce spatial churn, at the cost of looser bounds.

The [Boids example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/boids.html) demonstrates aggregation in a complete effect. Profile construction as well as query costs before increasing depth or rebuild frequency.

## GPU: ParticleSpatialGrid

Modules normally request a managed grid instead of constructing one. Set `useSpatialGrid: true`
for defaults or pass construction options through `spatialGridOptions`; the module's `modifyGPU` callback receives the
grid through `context.spatialGrid`. The equivalent CPU callback reads `context.octree` when
`useOctree` or `octreeOptions` is configured. Boids uses this managed lifecycle with its own
aggregate format and includes particle-affector source tags in the tree population;
its GPU grid uses the same managed acquisition and cleanup as other modules.

```ts
const neighbors = new Module(
  (particle, deltaTime, { system, octree }) => {
    const neighbors = octree.particlesInRadius(particle.position, 2);
    // Compare CPU neighbors; skip particle itself when needed.
  },
  {
    useOctree: true,
    useSpatialGrid: true,
    spatialGridOptions: { brickSubdivisions: 3, cellSubdivisions: 4 },
    modifyGPU: (particle, deltaTime, { spatialGrid: grid }) => {
      grid?.forEachParticleInRadius(
        particle.position,
        float(2),
        (neighbor, distanceSquared) => {
          // Build TSL operations using neighbor and distanceSquared.
        },
        { excludeIndex: particle.index },
      );
    },
  },
);
```

Custom infrastructure can instantiate `ParticleSpatialGrid` directly, call `rebuild` with a
WebGPU renderer and `GPUParticleBufferState`, then dispose it explicitly. A positive
`maxQuerySteps` truncates traversal; zero is unbounded. Automatic bounds expansion prevents lost
particles, but because the number of cells is fixed, expanding bounds increases cell size and
reduces spatial resolution. Keep bounds tight enough for the expected population and use
`readDiagnostics` only for validation or profiling because it performs asynchronous GPU readback.

# Renderer Children and Population LOD

Set `ParticleSystem.lod` to reduce simulated population with distance. The system calculates one `quality` value from zero through one and shares it with every emitter and renderer.

```ts
import { CompensationMode, Emitter, ParticleSystem, SpriteRenderer } from '@rzmps/rzmps';

const system = new ParticleSystem({
  lod: { distance: 20, quality: 0.5, maxLevel: 3, continuous: true },
  emitters: new Emitter({ rate: 200 }),
  renderers: new SpriteRenderer(undefined, {
    children: {
      count: 2,
      radius: 0.5,
      scale: [1, 0.6],
      alpha: [0.9, 0.5],
      randomizeScale: 0.2,
      randomizeAlpha: 0.15,
      radialFalloff: t => t * t,
    },
    compensation: CompensationMode.Children,
  }),
});
```

At quality 0.5, emission requests are halved before particles are allocated. Each birth receives a random priority below its birth quality, independent of its ID. When quality drops, particles at or above the new threshold are permanently removed before modules, movement, spatial queries, and collision. LOD removal does not dispatch normal death callbacks, death audio, or death subsystems. Surviving particles run every simulation step.

Increasing quality allows ordinary emission to restore density. Finite bursts may never recover their omitted particles. `simulationDistance` remains an independent hard cutoff, and `maxParticles` limits simulation capacity.

## Artistic children

The base `Renderer` expands its visual population before passing it to a renderer implementation. Each child inherits its immediate parent's attributes; only its position, scale, and alpha receive artistic modifiers. Children never enter `system.particles`, run modules, collide, or cause lifecycle events.

`renderer.renderedChildCount` reports additional artistic and LOD children. CPU counts update each frame. Reading this property during native GPU processing requests asynchronous diagnostics from the small counters buffer, at most four times per second; it does not read particle data back. The demo adds rendered and child totals to its particle counter only when children are present.

`count` is a timeless dynamic number: constants, ranges, and sets use deterministic per-parent selection. Counts are floored and clamped to nonnegative integers. They do not depend on age. A `[1, 3]` range normally produces one or two children. Zero is the default.

`radius` is the maximum spherical displacement, in particle simulation coordinates. Offsets remain fixed relative to the parent's position and do not rotate with its orientation. The default radius is zero.

`scale` and `alpha` are radial `ValueByParameter` multipliers. Numeric child multipliers are constants; ranges and callbacks vary with normalized radial distance. Both default to one. Each property's parameter is `clamp(distance / radius + randomize * (random - 0.5), 0, 1)`, followed by `radialFalloff`. Radius zero supplies distance zero. Randomization defaults to zero and easing defaults to linear. Scale and alpha use independent random streams, so changing alpha randomness does not move or resize a child.

Callbacks and easing use the existing GPU sampled-curve convention. TSL nodes are GPU-only and follow the existing dynamic-value compatibility rules.

## Compensation

`compensation` defaults to `CompensationMode.None`.

- `Size` multiplies visual scale by `1 / sqrt(quality)`, approximating constant billboard area. Simulated scale remains unchanged.
- `Children` adds approximately `1 / quality - 1` additional children to every original and artistic child. Fractional copies use deterministic selection. LOD copies inherit scale and opacity without further artistic modifiers.

There are exactly two generation stages. LOD children do not create further children. Quality zero generates no compensation copies. At quality 0.5, one simulated particle with two artistic children produces six visual instances.

The particle system owns compensation spacing. CPU views share a shallow `ParticleOctree` and cached per-root estimates; native GPU views share a `ParticleSpatialGrid` and a GPU spacing pass. The spatial structures inspect a bounded sample of local simulated neighbors. Estimates are retained for a root particle's lifetime to avoid offset jitter. Isolated particles fall back to their visual extent, so expanding system bounds cannot scatter compensation children. Spatial preparation runs only when compensation needs it, and CPU trees rebuild only when new roots need estimates.

## Identity and backend behavior

CPU particles expose `id`, `isChild`, `parent`, and `root`. Simulated particles have a null parent and are their own root. Child IDs derive from the immediate parent's identity and child ordinal. The base renderer uses `Particle.shallowClone(id, overrides)` for each visual child. Inherited vectors, colors, tags, custom data, and simulation snapshots are shared read-only. Each child owns its position; artistic scale modifiers and size compensation copy scale before modifying it. LOD children share their immediate parent’s scale and color. Child IDs use namespaced strings such as `root[0]`, `root[1]`, and `root[0][0]`. Artistic and LOD children share one ordinal sequence per parent; a root's LOD children follow its artistic children. Timeless seeded evaluation keeps counts and offsets stable across updates. Trails use the same stable child IDs to preserve independent histories.

Use `shallowClone` for a read-only view with selected replacements. Override vectors and colors are used directly, while unspecified references remain shared:

```ts
const view = particle.shallowClone('visual-copy', {
  position: particle.position.clone().add(offset),
  alpha: particle.alpha * 0.5,
});
```

`shallowClone` preserves the particle prototype and skips constructor work, ID generation, and new simulation snapshots. Renderers and custom consumers must avoid mutating shared attributes. Use `clone()` when independent mutable particle attributes are required.

GPU simulation contexts expose a computed slot/generation identity. Expanded render contexts resolve child identities and immediate/root views through one compact parent-index/ordinal mapping, with at most two hierarchy lookups. On GPU, guard dynamic parent access with `isChild`; original render slots resolve their parent view to themselves because shader-side null references do not exist. Simulation contexts have a null parent.

GPU-native sprites and meshes consume temporary packed visual buffers without reading child data back to the CPU. Artistic and LOD children occupy successive compact segments. Atomic allocation order may change packing, while identities remain independent of packing. Indirect draws use the GPU-produced visual range. Buffers are reused and grow in aggregate rather than reserving each parent's maximum possible count.

As with simulation storage, GPU visual storage has a practical capacity. The reusable arena reserves from the count distribution's mean, variance, and largest outlier and is bounded by `maxStorageBufferBindingSize`. Numeric TSL constants and uniforms use their current values; opaque GPU expressions reserve the full device-bounded arena because their counts cannot be bounded on CPU. Writes outside its capacity are discarded and counted internally. Very large or unbounded TSL count distributions should be avoided. CPU readback renderers, including trails, lights, and audio, keep their existing readback mechanism and expand children on CPU.

The generated compute and render shaders must fit the default eight-storage-buffer limit. `npm run preview -- --example lodStress --backend webgpu` records actual generated shader binding counts and active processing backend in its metadata.

Custom renderers implement `_update` for CPU input and `_updateGPU` for native GPU input. The public `update` and `updateGPU` methods perform base-class preprocessing before calling these hooks.

## Migration

Remove the former update-rate LOD settings from systems, emitters, modules, and renderers. Put distance/falloff/quality settings in `ParticleSystem.lod`. Replace renderer size compensation with `compensation: CompensationMode.Size`, or choose `Children` for density approximation. Emitter and renderer count selection are now coordinated by the simulated population; modules always update survivors at their normal frequency.

# Spatial Effects and Module Collections

A generic `SpatialEffect` is an Object3D containing a volume or custom test and a modifier. Add it to the same Three.js scene as the particle system. The system discovers scene effects when `useSpatialEffects` is enabled, then combines them with its modules in priority order. The effect's transform places its volume in the scene; RZMPS converts particle positions for tests.

The `spatialEffects` constructor collection supplies explicit effects in addition to scene discovery. `spatialEffectFilter` narrows the generic effects that can modify a system. Avoid using a broad filter that accidentally excludes your intended field. Use `tags` and `condition` on an effect to select particles after the effect has been selected.

Modules can collect scene effects for their own algorithms. Set `requireSpatialEffects` to one or more SpatialEffect constructors; `prepare()` traverses the scene and fills the module's `spatialEffects` list with matching instances. This is how specialized modules such as Boids can consume affectors without the affectors also acting as generic modifiers.

For a module, explicitly supplying `spatialEffects: []` deliberately gives it an empty collection and suppresses discovery. Supplying a nonempty collection limits it to those objects. `spatialEffectFilter` and constructor requirements still filter that explicit list. Distinguish this module-level selection from the system's generic effects list.

Use [First Spatial Effect](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/first-spatial-effect.html) to build a field. For expensive selection, cache work in `prepare()`
rather than traversing the scene inside every particle callback. If you override `prepare()`, call
`super.prepare(context)` when you rely on the base spatial collection behavior.

On GPU, built-in analytic effects can be parameterized, batched, and indexed together. A custom
effect must provide GPU callbacks to run there; an unsupported generic effect is skipped rather
than forcing the whole system to CPU. Geometry-backed custom effects can use a baked inclusion
field, and `updatePolicy` distinguishes static, transform-only, and deforming geometry updates.
Optional system bounds filtering applies only to effects whose built-in geometry test guarantees
that bounds overlap is meaningful. See [GPU processing](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/gpu-processing.html) for callback signatures
and update policies.

# Using Subsystems

Attach a secondary ParticleSystem with `parent.addSubSystem(child, options)`. The parent owns its simulation timing;
update only the root. The child is reused across emissions, with separate emission contexts for parent particles, rather
than creating a new system for every event.

Choose `emitOnSpawn`, `emitOnDeath`, or `emitOnCollision` for event bursts. Use `emitContinuous` for a stream following
live parent particles. A burst emitter with `rate: 0` and a time-zero burst is a good starting point for a short event
effect. A continuous smoke emitter needs a rate and a lifetime long enough to leave a visible wake.

Inheritance factors control scale, lifetime, color, alpha, mass, and velocity transferred from the triggering particle.
Set `inheritLifetime: 0` when a death burst should keep its own lifetime; inheriting a dying particle's lifetime would
defeat the separate timing. Set `inheritScale: 0` when the secondary effect should retain a fixed world size. `ratio`
samples which parent particles emit; lowering it reduces child population and renderer costs.

Collision emission needs a Collision module and collidable scene geometry or a configured collision backend.
`impulseThreshold` rejects weak contacts; impulse factors can increase spark scale or speed, and
`impulseAffectsAlignment` points emission away from the contact. Test in a collision scene: an empty scene cannot
demonstrate a contact-triggered effect.

[Fireworks](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireworks.html) combines continuous rocket smoke and a death burst. [Metal
Balls](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/collisionSubEmitters.html) combines collision sparks and collision audio. Inspect their source-linked
system regions as well as their emitter regions: the child's lifetime, gravity, and looping choices are independent of
the parent.

Destroy the owning root to clean up the effect. Do not also update owned subsystems from a scene traversal, or attempt
to reuse one child under two parents. Explicit frame advancement follows the same parent-owned event processing as
normal updates.

GPU-active roots schedule subsystem systems parent-before-child and keep native spawn, death,
collision, and continuous runs in GPU buffers. CPU listeners and CPU-input renderers receive
asynchronous event/readback data and can observe a small delay. A function-valued `shouldEmit`
cannot be translated automatically to a GPU predicate; inspect `getGPUEmissionSupport()` when a
custom subsystem selector is involved.

Registered sources and named custom events also drive these same subsystem contexts. Use `tags`
to select eligible source tags and `onEvent` for CPU or native GPU context handlers. See
[Emission Sources and Custom Events](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/emission-sources-events.html) and
[Acid](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/acid.html).

## Simulation frames

`simulationSpace` selects the reference frame for particle motion:

| Mode | Frame |
| --- | --- |
| `'world'` | Identity world matrix. Existing particles stay behind when the system moves. |
| `'local'` | The particle system's world transform. |
| `'transform'` | `simulationSpaceTransform`, supplied as an Object3D or world Matrix4; omitted means identity. |
| `'source'` | Each particle's emitting source transform. On a root system, this behaves like Local. |

Transform mode keeps a live reference. Moving the supplied Object3D, including its ancestors, or editing the supplied
world Matrix4 moves existing particles with that frame. The emitter still belongs to the particle system: its world
pose is converted into the selected simulation frame at birth. A source is a per-particle version of this relationship,
so one shared subsystem can attach particles to many moving sources.

```js
const pulses = new ParticleSystem({
  simulationSpace: 'source',
  sourceLoss: 'kill',
  // emitters, modules, renderers...
});
fireflies.addSubSystem(pulses, {
  onEvent: ['flash'],
  inheritLifetime: 0,
  inheritScale: 0,
});
```

Source particles keep their sampled offsets and independent motion while following source translation, rotation, and
inherited scale. `inheritScale: 0` keeps the attachment frame's scale at one. This avoids a follow module, source maps,
or storing source identity in application-owned particle attributes. Both registered sources and simulated particles
work; native GPU sources use slot and generation handles without copying their transforms through the CPU.

`sourceLoss` defaults to `'detach'`: an existing particle stops following the lost source and continues from its last
resolved pose. Choose `'kill'` for effects that should disappear with their source, such as firefly pulses. Reusing a
GPU
slot never reattaches an old particle to its replacement. Delayed births from a lost source are canceled; a death event
instead emits from its final snapshot and creates unattached particles. Singular reference matrices retain the last
usable frame for existing attachments. Use nonzero scales for emission.

Source space permits motion relative to the source. To pin a particle to its sampled offset, set the emitter's
`radialSpeed: 0` and leave its initial velocity and inherited velocity at zero; movement modules can also move it away
from that offset. The emitter's default radial speed is 1, including in Source space.

An explicitly configured child space survives parenting and parent space changes. A child with no explicit space
inherits its parent's mode, including its Transform reference when no child reference is supplied. For example, a
World parent gives an unspecified child World space, while an explicitly configured Source child stays in Source space.
Assigning `child.simulationSpace` also makes that child's choice explicit. This replaces the previous forced matching
of parent and child modes; emission converts between their frames when they differ. Changing the mode
or replacing `simulationSpaceTransform` preserves the world pose of existing particles; moving the referenced transform
moves the effect. GPU conversion takes place at the next simulation step.

Modules, particle positions, spatial queries, collisions, renderer inputs, and readback use a shared resolved coordinate
space: World uses world coordinates, Transform uses the supplied frame, and Local/Source use the system's coordinates.
Source offsets and motion are transformed into that common space before module updates. Consequently neighbor queries
can compare particles emitted by different sources, and scene forces act in the common frame. Use
`simulationToWorld`, `worldToSimulation`, and `getSimulationToWorldMatrix` for application conversions;
`resolveSimulationFrame(particle)` also includes a CPU particle's attachment frame. Three.js `localToWorld` and
`worldToLocal` continue to describe the Object3D itself. Particle orientation and scale use TRS decomposition;
compositions that introduce shear have the same approximation as Three.js Object3D transforms.

See [Fireflies](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireflies.html) for native Source attachments and
[Emission Sources and Custom Events](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/guides/emission-sources-events.html) for registered origins and payload handlers.

# Using Tags

Tags divide one particle population into independently styled or modified groups. An emitter assigns tags when particles are born. A module or renderer with a tag filter accepts particles sharing a selected tag; a component without a tag selection applies to the whole population.

`tagSelection: 'all'` assigns the supplied tags together. Use `'distribute'` to cycle through them, giving separate particles separate tags. A particle carrying both `spheres` and `cubes` would match both renderers; distributed assignment avoids rendering each particle twice in the [Cubes and Spheres example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/tags.html).

That example uses a single emitter at 12 particles per second. Cube particles rotate and fade, while sphere particles grow and collide. Sprite and mesh renderers filter by the same tag names. This keeps emission timing and system ownership shared while changing appearance and behavior.

A `condition` callback further restricts a module or spatial effect after tag matching. Use it for a value-dependent rule, such as age or speed, instead of creating a tag for every transient state. Keep conditions cheap because they run over the candidate population each update.

Tags are application-defined values. Use consistent names across emitters, module filters, renderer filters, and particle-affector `sourceTags`. A misspelled tag can produce a technically valid but invisible effect; inspect both the population and the rendered preview when diagnosing it.

## Changing Tags During Updates

CPU modules can modify `particle.tags` directly. GPU update callbacks can use `particle.addTag(name)` and
`particle.removeTag(name)` to modify the particle's bitmask without assigning bit positions themselves:

```ts
const pulseTags = new Module(() => {}, {
  modifyGPU(particle) {
    If(particle.alpha.greaterThan(0.5), () => {
      particle.addTag('glowing');
    }).Else(() => {
      particle.removeTag('glowing');
    });
  },
});
const lights = new LightRenderer({ tags: 'glowing', count: 16 });
```

Here `If` comes from `three/tsl`; `Module` and `LightRenderer` come from `@rzmps/rzmps`. The tag must already be
registered by an emitter, module, renderer, spatial effect, or subsystem tag selector in the composition. The light
renderer registers `glowing` in this example. Unknown names throw during shader construction, so typos cannot silently
change unrelated bits. Repeated additions and removals are idempotent and preserve other tags, including bit 31.

Use a permanent module priority when the change should persist into later simulation steps. A transient module's
changes follow the existing transient-state rules. GPU event records are snapshots; their source views cannot use
these helpers to mutate a live particle. GPU tag capacity remains 32 names per composition.

The [Fireflies example](https://rzmps.rzmay.com/docs/examples/fireflies.html) gives its glow pulses their own particle system, allowing a light
renderer to select that population directly without changing tags.


Sub-particles do not automatically inherit tags from their source particle or registered source. Set the child
emitter's `tags` explicitly. `sourceTags` filters event origins independently of the tags assigned to new particles;
this makes it possible to select rocket deaths while producing sparkles that do not match the rocket filter.
Tag inheritance is not required for Source simulation space or source tracking.
